title: Bihar Porter Sold Land to Send Sons to Kota; Both Cracked NEET and JEE
excerpt: Manoj Kumar of Gaya sold one of his family's two plots to fund two years of coaching. Sonu Raj scored 636 in NEET and entered AIIMS CAPFIMS in Delhi; Monu Raj reached BIT Mesra despite months of illness.
body:
• Manoj Kumar, who works as a porter in the grain market in Gaya, Bihar, sold one of his family's two small plots of land to fund two years of entrance-exam coaching in Kota for his two sons.
  • Elder son Sonu Raj scored 636 marks in NEET-UG 2026 in his first attempt and has taken admission at the AIIMS Central Armed Police Forces Institute of Medical Sciences (CAPFIMS) in Delhi.
  • Younger son Monu Raj scored 93 percentile in JEE Main and has joined the Chemical Engineering programme at the Birla Institute of Technology, Mesra, in Ranchi.
  • Monu prepared through typhoid, jaundice and a fever that lasted nearly three months during the two years the brothers lived and studied together in Kota.

For Manoj Kumar, the arithmetic of his sons' ambitions came down to two small plots of land. The plots grew grain the family ate and sold for a little cash. He sold one of them — half of everything the family owned — so that Sonu Raj and Monu Raj could spend two years in Kota, Rajasthan, preparing for the medical and engineering entrance examinations. This year, both admissions came through.

Sonu Raj, the elder brother, scored 636 marks in NEET-UG 2026 in his first attempt and qualified for the AIIMS Central Armed Police Forces Institute of Medical Sciences (CAPFIMS) in Delhi, according to Education Times. Monu Raj scored 93 percentile in JEE Main and secured a Chemical Engineering seat at the Birla Institute of Technology (BIT), Mesra, in Ranchi.

Work that paid for the dream

Kumar works as a porter in the grain and paddy market in Gaya, earning commission by helping farmers sell their crops; before that he worked as a daily-wage labourer under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), ITDC India reported. His wife, Reshmi Devi, is a homemaker. The household relied on irregular, low-wage earnings, and the two plots were its primary productive asset.

When the brothers set their sights on Kota — Monu says he was inspired by watching earlier students from Gaya return as doctors and engineers — the cost of coaching, housing and study material was beyond what portering could pay. Kumar sold one plot to cover the relocation and tuition at Allen Career Institute, where both brothers enrolled.

"Our hard work and sacrifices have finally borne fruit."

— Manoj Kumar

Two years in Kota, one of them through illness

The brothers lived together in Kota for two years of preparation. For Monu, much of that period ran alongside serious illness: he contracted typhoid, then jaundice, and suffered episodes of abnormally rapid heartbeat with a fever that lasted nearly three months, Education Times reported. He kept attending classes through it and cleared the JEE Main cutoff for BIT Mesra.

Monu had been a strong student before Kota — 96 percent in Class 10 and 84.5 percent in Class 12. "Seeing several students from Gaya go to Kota to prepare for JEE and NEET and eventually become engineers and doctors inspired me to dream big," he said.

"We worked hard to prepare for the exams and fulfil our parents' dreams. Our parents always wanted us to get the best of education for which they underwent hardship."

— Sonu Raj

What the results change

Sonu is now set to train as a doctor in Delhi and Monu to study chemical engineering in Ranchi — the two professions the family had aimed at when the land was sold. Allen founder Naveen Maheshwari said students like the brothers "become examples of social transformation and inspire other students to move forward and pursue their dreams." For the family in Gaya, the remaining plot now stands next to a different asset: two professional degrees in progress, bought with the other one.
